positions/three-self-indigenous-principl: The indigenous ("three-self") principle
Three-self formula
Nevius plan
Indigenous church principle
Venn–Anderson formula
Missions should plant churches that are self-supporting, self-governing and self-propagating from as early as possible, with local leaders, so that the foreign mission can withdraw.
The goal of mission is a mature local church, not a permanent mission station.
Foreign money and control create dependency and stunt growth.
Local believers should evangelise their own people.
Paul’s practice of appointing elders and moving on is the model (Allen).
Titus 1:5
1 Thessalonians 1:8
2 Timothy 2:2

Formulated in the 1840s–50s by Henry Venn of the CMS and Rufus Anderson of the ABCFM; applied by John Nevius (Methods of Mission Work, 1886) and in Korea from 1890; advocated by Roland Allen (Missionary Methods: St Paul’s or Ours?, 1912). In China the terminology was co-opted by the state’s Three-Self Patriotic Movement (1954).
Rufus Anderson
Roland Allen
Melvin Hodges (Pentecostal)
Wu Yaozong (Three-Self, China)
Korean Protestantism, built on the Nevius plan, became one of the strongest indigenous churches in Asia.
It follows Paul’s method of short stays and local elders.
It counters colonial paternalism by entrusting authority to local Christians.
In practice missions often delayed handover for generations on paternalistic grounds (as in the undermining of Crowther).
The Chinese state’s use of "three-self" shows the language can serve political control.
Some argue a fourth "self", self-theologising (Hiebert), was neglected, and that interdependence is better than independence.
Advocates reply that failures of implementation confirm rather than refute the principle.
Many now speak of partnership and interdependence while keeping local ownership.
Strong indigenous churches in Korea, Nigeria, Uganda and elsewhere.
Background to the Three-Self Patriotic Movement and its rejection by house churches.
Influence on Pentecostal mission strategy (Hodges, The Indigenous Church, 1953).
positions/translation-principle/name: Translatability and world Christianity (defence of mission against the colonial critique)
positions/translation-principle/oneLine: Christianity has no sacred language or single home culture; by translating Scripture into every vernacular, missions, despite colonial entanglements, empowered local peoples to receive the gospel on their own terms, producing a genuinely world Christianity.
positions/translation-principle/coreClai: Pentecost’s many tongues show that every language can carry revelation.
Translation relativises the missionary’s culture and dignifies the receptor culture.
Converts and local evangelists, not foreign missionaries, did most of the work of spreading the faith.
Missions often opposed colonial abuses and promoted literacy, education and civil society.
The colonial critique is real but incomplete: Christianity grew fastest after decolonisation.
positions/translation-principle/origin: Articulated by Andrew Walls (essays from the 1970s; The Missionary Movement in Christian History, 1996) and Lamin Sanneh (Translating the Message, 1989), developed by Kwame Bediako, Dana Robert, Brian Stanley (The Bible and the Flag, 1990) and quantitatively by Robert Woodberry (2012), in response to postcolonial critiques of mission.
positions/translation-principle/stronges: Unlike Islam’s Arabic Qur’an, Christian Scripture has always been translated, from the Septuagint to over 700 complete Bibles.
African and Asian Christianity exploded after missionaries and colonial rulers left (e.g. Africa from about 10 million Christians in 1900 to over 600 million today).
Mission schools trained many leaders of independence movements; Woodberry finds Protestant missions correlated with later democracy.
Postcolonial historians (e.g. Jean and John Comaroff) argue that missions colonised consciousness, imposing Western norms in dress, family and economy.
Missionaries often depended on and legitimated colonial rule, and racial hierarchies persisted inside mission churches.
Emphasising agency of converts can minimise real harms such as residential schools in Canada and Australia.
positions/translation-principle/response: Walls and Sanneh do not deny complicity; they argue the message escaped its messengers, as seen in African Initiated Churches.
Stanley shows that relations between missions and empire were ambivalent, with missionaries both collaborating and opposing colonial interests.
positions/translation-principle/conseque: Reframed missiology and church history as "world Christianity".
Encouraged study of African and Asian agency in Christian expansion.
Continuing debate with postcolonial and Indigenous critiques of mission.
positions/missio-dei/oneLine: Mission is first God’s own activity: the Father sends the Son and the Spirit, and the triune God sends the Church; the Church does not have a mission so much as God’s mission has a Church.
positions/missio-dei/coreClaims/0: Mission is rooted in the Trinity’s sending (John 20:21).
positions/missio-dei/coreClaims/1: The Church is by nature missionary (Ad Gentes 2), not merely a sender of missionaries.
positions/missio-dei/coreClaims/2: God is at work in the world beyond the Church, and the Church joins that work.
positions/missio-dei/coreClaims/3: Mission includes proclamation, service, justice and care for creation (in broader versions).
positions/missio-dei/coreClaims/4: Western societies are themselves mission fields (Newbigin, missional church).
positions/missio-dei/origin: Prepared by Karl Barth’s 1932 lecture on mission and the Trinity, crystallised at the IMC conference at Willingen (1952) and named by Karl Hartenstein; broadened in WCC circles (Uppsala 1968) toward "humanisation"; developed by David Bosch (Transforming Mission, 1991), Lesslie Newbigin and the "missional church" movement (Guder, 1998).
positions/missio-dei/strongestArguments/: Scripture presents mission as God’s initiative from Abraham to Pentecost, not a human programme.
It overcomes the split between "church" and "mission" and between home and foreign mission.
It places the Church in humility under God’s purposes, chastened after colonial missions.
positions/missio-dei/strongestObjections: Evangelical critics argue that ecumenical versions dissolved mission into social and political action, losing evangelism (Uppsala 1968 controversy).
If God is active everywhere, the concept can become so broad that "if everything is mission, nothing is mission" (Stephen Neill).
Some theologians argue the Trinitarian "sending" analogy is used loosely.
positions/missio-dei/responses/0: Advocates such as Bosch and Christopher Wright insist that missio Dei includes the proclamation of Christ as its heart.
positions/missio-dei/responses/1: Catholic and evangelical uses root it firmly in the Church’s proclamation and sacraments.
positions/missio-dei/consequences/0: Integration of the IMC into the WCC (1961).
positions/missio-dei/consequences/1: Missional church movement in Western post-Christendom contexts.
positions/missio-dei/consequences/2: Common vocabulary across Catholic (Ad Gentes), Orthodox and Protestant missiology.
positions/integral-mission/oneLine: The gospel of the kingdom addresses the whole person and the whole of society, so evangelism and social responsibility are inseparable partners in the church’s mission.
positions/integral-mission/coreClaims/0: Jesus proclaimed and enacted the kingdom: preaching, healing, feeding and confronting injustice (Luke 4:18–19).
positions/integral-mission/coreClaims/1: Social action is not merely a bridge to evangelism but part of obedience to Christ.
positions/integral-mission/coreClaims/2: Western evangelism was often captive to individualism and consumerism.
positions/integral-mission/coreClaims/3: The church community itself embodies the gospel.
positions/integral-mission/origin: Raised by René Padilla and Samuel Escobar at Lausanne (1974) and developed by the Latin American Theological Fraternity (founded 1970); expressed in the Micah Declaration (2001) and the Cape Town Commitment (2010). Parallel Catholic emphasis in Evangelii Nuntiandi (1975) and Pentecostal social engagement.
positions/integral-mission/strongestArgu: Jesus’ own ministry combined word and deed inseparably.
Integral mission has credibility among the poor in Latin America, Africa and Asia.
It answers the charge that evangelicals cared only for souls.
positions/integral-mission/strongestObje: Some evangelicals fear it leads, as in parts of the ecumenical movement, to a social gospel that neglects conversion.
Critics argue social transformation belongs mainly to Christians’ vocations rather than the institutional church’s mission.
Liberationists sometimes see it as too cautious about structural and political change.
positions/integral-mission/responses/0: Padilla and Stott insisted that evangelism remains central and that the kingdom is God’s work, not a human utopia.
positions/integral-mission/responses/1: They answer liberationist critics that the church must remain free from partisan ideologies.
positions/integral-mission/consequences/: Evangelical relief and development agencies (e.g. Tearfund, World Vision’s theological framework).
Micah Network (1999) and Cape Town Commitment (2010).
A distinctive Latin American evangelical theology.
positions/exclusivism-particularism/oneL: Jesus Christ is the unique and final revelation of God and the only saviour; other religions, however noble, are not paths to salvation, and the Church must call all people to faith in him.
positions/exclusivism-particularism/core: Salvation is only through the person and work of Jesus Christ (Acts 4:12; John 14:6).
Other religions contain truths through general revelation and common grace but also error and rebellion; they do not save.
Truth claims of religions conflict and cannot all be correct (Netland).
Mission and evangelism are therefore urgent.
Particularists differ on whether explicit knowledge of Christ is required (restrictivism) or not (wider hope).
positions/exclusivism-particularism/orig: The dominant patristic, medieval and Reformation conviction; restated against pluralism by Karl Barth (Church Dogmatics I/2, §17, 1938), Hendrik Kraemer at Tambaram (1938), the Frankfurt Declaration (1970), the Lausanne Covenant (1974) and Lesslie Newbigin (1989).
positions/exclusivism-particularism/stro: The New Testament repeatedly presents Christ as the unique and exclusive way.
Pluralism cannot account for the incarnation and resurrection as once-for-all events.
Contradictory claims (e.g. on God’s personhood, Christ’s death) cannot all be true.
It seems to consign the majority of humanity, including those who never heard of Christ, to damnation (the problem of the unevangelised).
Pluralists argue that religious belief largely depends on birthplace, making exclusive claims arbitrary.
Its history is entangled with intolerance and coercion.
positions/exclusivism-particularism/resp: Particularists answer that God’s justice and mercy toward the unevangelised can be trusted (Gen 18:25), and some hold a wider hope.
They argue that pluralism is itself a particular, Western-liberal claim, and that Christian particularity can coexist with respect and religious liberty (Newbigin).
positions/exclusivism-particularism/cons: Underpins evangelical, Pentecostal and much Orthodox and Catholic missionary motivation.
Ongoing debates on interfaith relations and proselytism.
positions/restrictivism/oneLine: Only those who hear the gospel and explicitly believe in Christ (and, in the Catholic form, are joined to the Church) can be saved; those who die without such faith are lost.
positions/restrictivism/coreClaims/0: Faith comes by hearing the word of Christ (Rom 10:14–17); without hearing there is no saving faith.
positions/restrictivism/coreClaims/1: All are condemned in Adam and "without excuse" before general revelation (Rom 1:20).
positions/restrictivism/coreClaims/2: There is no salvation outside the Church (Cyprian; Florence, 1442).
positions/restrictivism/coreClaims/3: This fact gives mission its urgency.
positions/restrictivism/origin: Cyprian (c.256), Fulgentius of Ruspe, Boniface VIII’s Unam Sanctam (1302) and the Council of Florence (1442); widely held by Reformation and modern Protestants; in strict Catholic form taught by Leonard Feeney and rejected by Rome (1949); defended by evangelicals such as Ronald Nash (Is Jesus the Only Savior?, 1994).
positions/restrictivism/strongestArgumen: Romans 10 explicitly ties salvation to hearing and believing the gospel.
The Book of Acts shows even devout seekers (Cornelius) needing to hear about Christ.
It preserves the urgency of mission that drove Carey and Taylor.
positions/restrictivism/strongestObjecti: It seems to make salvation depend on geographical and historical accident, which critics call incompatible with God’s love (1 Tim 2:4).
Old Testament believers and "holy pagans" (Melchizedek, Job, Rahab) were saved without knowing Jesus by name.
Catholic teaching since 1949 and Vatican II has rejected the strict reading.
positions/restrictivism/responses/0: Restrictivists answer that Old Testament believers trusted God’s promised redeemer, a special revelation unavailable to modern unevangelised peoples.
positions/restrictivism/responses/1: They argue that God justly condemns sinners and that the remedy is mission, not speculation about other ways.
positions/restrictivism/consequences/0: Strong motive for evangelical and earlier Catholic missions.
positions/restrictivism/consequences/1: Moral and theological objections that fuelled inclusivism and pluralism.
positions/restrictivism/consequences/2: The Feeney controversy and Catholic clarification (1949).
